Package org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter

Class CsrfBoundary

java.lang.Object
org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter.CsrfBoundary
All Implemented Interfaces:
RequestBoundary
public class CsrfBoundary extends Object implements RequestBoundary
The cross-site request forgery boundary for an application reachable from the network: decides whether a state-changing request came from this application's own page, or from a client that is not a browser, and refuses it when it came from some other site's page.
What this answers, and what it does not

This class answers one question:

Did this request come from this app's own page, or from a non-browser client?

It does not answer who is the caller (authentication) or did the user mean it (intent). A user who has the application's own page open, and is induced to click something on it, produces a request that passes every check here. Intent needs its own, separate gate.

For an application bound only to the loopback interface, LoopbackBoundary pins a single known origin and is stricter. This class is for applications whose own origin is whatever the request's Host says it is.

The checks

check(HttpServletRequest) runs these steps in order, and the first failure wins. The method judged is the effective method, so a method query parameter or an override header cannot carry a write past them.

StepApplies toRefused whenReasonStatus
Allowed hostsEvery request, when CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...) is set The request's own host is not listed; or its Host (on HTTP/2, its :authority) is missing or malformed HOST_NOT_ALLOWED; HOST_MISSING, HOST_MALFORMED Not listed: 421; missing or malformed Host: 400
Safe methodGET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE Never: allowed
Own originUnsafe requests Host (on HTTP/2, :authority) is absent, repeated, or not a host with an optional port HOST_MISSING, HOST_MALFORMED400
PeerUnsafe requests, and safe ones when allowedHosts is set, when CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedProxies(String...) is set The peer is not in the allow-list and the request carries a forwarded host in the selected family; without one, the request is judged on the container's own view instead FORWARDED_PEER_NOT_TRUSTED403
Forwarded originUnsafe requests, and safe ones when allowedHosts is set, when CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedForwarding(ForwardedSource) is on The forwarded host or proto is missing, malformed, or has fewer or unequal entries than the trusted hop count; or the container's view disagrees with it FORWARDED_HOST_MISSING, FORWARDED_PROTO_MISSING, FORWARDED_HOST_MALFORMED, FORWARDED_PROTO_MALFORMED, FORWARDED_HOPS_INSUFFICIENT, FORWARDED_HOPS_MISMATCH, FORWARDED_CONTAINER_MISMATCH403
Origin presentUnsafe requests The literal null; or repeated, unparseable or not this server's own origin; or Sec-Fetch-Site present and not exactly same-origin ORIGIN_NULL, ORIGIN_MISMATCH, FETCH_SITE_NOT_SAME_ORIGIN403
Origin absentUnsafe requests Sec-Fetch-Site present and not exactly same-origin; or, with no fetch metadata either, the non-browser policy refuses it FETCH_SITE_NOT_SAME_ORIGIN, SIMPLE_REQUEST_WITHOUT_ORIGIN, ORIGIN_MISSING 403
Browser requestUnsafe requests from a page CsrfBoundary.Builder.requireJson(boolean) is on and the type is not JSON; or the token header is missing, or does not verify CONTENT_TYPE_NOT_JSON (415), CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING, CSRF_TOKEN_MISMATCH 403

Origins are compared as normalized (scheme, host, port) triples, never as raw text: scheme and host are lower-cased (ASCII only), an absent port means the scheme's default, and an explicit port is decimal with no sign and no leading zero. Nothing else is re-canonicalized, so 127.1, [::ffff:127.0.0.1] and a trailing dot each fail to match any other spelling of the same address. That is fail-closed, by design.

Non-browser clients

A request with neither Origin nor Sec-Fetch-Site is handled by CsrfBoundary.Builder.nonBrowser(NonBrowser). The default, CsrfBoundary.NonBrowser.ADMIT_NON_SIMPLE, admits only requests a browser could not have sent cross-site without a CORS preflight, which this boundary never answers. That relies on browsers sending Origin on every non-simple request they issue; current browsers do, and the Origin check is the real control for them.

The token is accepted only in the header

The token is read from the csrfHeader() request header and nowhere else: never a query parameter, never a form field. A plain HTML <form> cannot set a header, so every HTML form POST, including the application's own, is refused with CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING. This boundary is for applications whose writes go through script that sends the header.

The request's own origin, and proxies

By default (CsrfBoundary.OriginSource.HOST_HEADER) the request's own origin is ServletRequest.getScheme() plus the Host header (on HTTP/2, the :authority; see below). X-Forwarded-* and Forwarded are never read by this class unless CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedForwarding(ForwardedSource) is set (see below). Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, use CsrfBoundary.OriginSource.CONTAINER and configure the container's own forwarded-header support; the boundary then takes the origin from getScheme(), getServerName() and getServerPort().

Under CONTAINER the boundary must run after the container's forwarded-header rewrite. Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer, Tomcat's RemoteIpValve and Spring Boot's forward-headers-strategy=native rewrite the request before any filter runs, so order does not matter. Spring Boot's forward-headers-strategy=framework registers ForwardedHeaderFilter at Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE, so this boundary's filter must be registered strictly later, never at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE itself. The boundary cannot see its own order; a misordered deployment shows up as scheme-mismatch refusals and the warning described below.

Trusting a forwarded origin

If your container cannot rewrite the request itself, or does not do so for WebSocket upgrades, use CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedForwarding(ForwardedSource). The request's own origin is then the forwarded host and proto of the one header family named (X-Forwarded-Host plus X-Forwarded-Proto, or host= plus proto= in one Forwarded element), on HTTP requests and WebSocket handshakes alike. The other family and X-Forwarded-Port are never read; put a non-default port in the host value.

  • Turn it on only if every request reaches the server through your proxy, and the proxy removes or appends after any client-supplied copy. A server clients can reach directly lets them choose the origin, and that defeats CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...) for reads.
  • Set CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedHops(int) to exactly the number of proxies that append. A chain of overwriting proxies stays at 1. Never set it higher: an overstated count trusts a value the client wrote.
  • A missing, malformed, short or misaligned value is refused (FORWARDED_*, 403), never guessed at, and nothing falls back to Host. A proxy that sets only X-Forwarded-Proto is not supported.
  • CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...) is checked against the forwarded host, so list the public names.
  • Under CsrfBoundary.OriginSource.CONTAINER the container's rewritten origin, port included, must equal the forwarded one, or the request is refused (FORWARDED_CONTAINER_MISMATCH); configure both to read the same header family and hop. Do not enable this where the container consumes the headers (Spring forward-headers-strategy=framework): every request is then refused as missing. Under CsrfBoundary.OriginSource.HOST_HEADER and on handshakes, a container host that equals an entry left of the selected one is refused too, because the container trusted a hop the client could have written.
  • A handshake is judged only through checkHandshake(String, HandshakeHosts, Map).
  • To believe the headers only from your proxy's own address, add CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedProxies(String...). A request from another peer that carries a forwarded host is refused (FORWARDED_PEER_NOT_TRUSTED); one that does not is judged on the container's view. It needs a container that reports the TCP peer (no RemoteIpValve, ForwardedRequestCustomizer or PROXY protocol). A handshake's peer comes from checkHandshake(String, HandshakeHosts, Map, java.net.InetAddress): Jetty supplies it, Tomcat does not, so on Tomcat a handshake that carries a forwarded host is refused while the list is set. Only the peer is checked: the allow-list does not walk X-Forwarded-For or for=, so a trusted proxy that appends behind another untrusted tier is still believed for what it wrote.
HTTP/2 and :authority

An HTTP/2 request has no Host header; its :authority pseudo-header plays that part, and servlet containers surface it only through ServletRequest.getServerName() and ServletRequest.getServerPort(). So that a deployment that speaks HTTP/2 keeps working, a request with no Host header whose ServletRequest.getProtocol() is exactly HTTP/2.0 is judged on its server name and port in Host's place, for both CsrfBoundary.OriginSources and for CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...). Any other request without a Host is still refused (HOST_MISSING). A request that does carry a Host header is judged on it as before.

The same holds for a WebSocket handshake carried over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441, extended CONNECT): with no Host, and no Sec-WebSocket-Key or Upgrade header to mark it an RFC 6455 request, the authority of the handshake's request URI stands in for Host. Jetty advertises RFC 8441 by default once HTTP/2 is enabled; Tomcat does not support it.

Because the server name is what the container's forwarded-header support rewrites, under CsrfBoundary.OriginSource.HOST_HEADER an HTTP/2 request is judged on the forwarded host when such support is enabled (Tomcat's RemoteIpValve with a host header, Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter, Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer). HOST_HEADER is therefore protocol-dependent: it reads the raw Host on HTTP/1.1 and the container's server name on HTTP/2. Enable forwarded-header support only behind a proxy that overwrites X-Forwarded-*, or list the expected hosts with CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...).

Non-goals
  • DNS rebinding, unless CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...) is set: a rebound page's Origin and Host agree. TLS defeats rebinding; a plain-HTTP intranet application should list its host names.
  • Cross-origin callers (CORS). Refused. The boundary adds no Access-Control-Allow-* header; do not put an origin-reflecting CORS layer in front of it.
  • Authentication, intent, session management. The boundary never changes a session id and never sets cookie attributes.
  • Script running inside the page (XSS, a malicious extension) passes every check.
  • HTML form POSTs and Referer checking.
  • Telling a trustworthy proxy from a client by anything but its address. The optional allow-list of CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedProxies(String...) checks the peer address and nothing more: it does not authenticate the proxy, and a client behind a listed address (a shared NAT, a sidecar) is believed too.
What an application must do
  • Call HttpServletRequest.changeSessionId() on login. A per-session token follows the session id, so without that a token seen before login stays valid after it.
  • Mark the session cookie HttpOnly and SameSite, and do not scope it to a parent Domain.
  • Not use URL rewriting for session ids.
Responses and logging

A rejection message names the header at fault and the kind of value expected. It never echoes a value the request presented, never prints this server's own origin, and never reveals whether a session exists. Each refusal is logged at FINE without the query string, the token header, Cookie or Authorization; the raw Origin and Host (and, for a FORWARDED_* refusal, the forwarded headers) appear only at FINEST, stripped of control characters and truncated. Three misconfiguration patterns are logged once per process at WARNING: a scheme-only mismatch, a port-only mismatch, and repeated missing tokens from the application's own origin.

Example:

CsrfBoundary boundary = CsrfBoundary.create() .allowedHosts("app.example.com") .build(); servletContext.addFilter("csrf", new RequestBoundaryFilter(boundary)) .addMappingForUrlPatterns(null, false, "/*");

    • acceptsHandshakeOrigin

      public boolean acceptsHandshakeOrigin(String origin)
      Whether a WebSocket handshake's Origin value is well-formed enough to be checked later, once the handshake's Host is visible.

      For a container's checkOrigin hook, which sees the Origin value and nothing else, so it can refuse the upgrade with 403 before it happens. A missing or blank value, the literal null, and anything that is not exactly scheme "://" host [":" port] with an http or https scheme are refused. A well-formed value says nothing yet about whether it is this server's own origin: that is checkHandshake(String, List, List, List)'s job.

      Parameters:
      origin - The Origin header value. Can be null.
      Returns:
      true if the value parses as an http(s) origin.

    • checkHandshake

      public BoundaryResult checkHandshake(String scheme, List<String> hosts, List<String> origins, List<String> fetchSites)
      Applies this boundary to a WebSocket handshake.

      A WebSocket upgrade is a GET, so check(HttpServletRequest) lets it through untouched; this method is the boundary for the upgrade instead. No token can be sent on a handshake, so the control is Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site:

      1. Host must be a single well-formed value (HOST_MISSING, HOST_MALFORMED). A handshake carried over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) has none, and its request URI's authority stands in; see HandshakeHosts.
      2. The handshake's own scheme comes from its request URI: ws is http, wss is https, and http or https are used as they are. Any other scheme, or none, means the handshake's own origin is unknown, and it is refused (ORIGIN_MISMATCH).
      3. When CsrfBoundary.Builder.allowedHosts(String...) is set, the Host must be one of them (HOST_NOT_ALLOWED).
      4. Origin must be a single value naming the same scheme, host and port as the handshake's own scheme and Host (ORIGIN_MISSING, ORIGIN_NULL, ORIGIN_MISMATCH).
      5. Sec-Fetch-Site, when present, must be a single same-origin value (FETCH_SITE_NOT_SAME_ORIGIN).

      With CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedForwarding(ForwardedSource) set, the forwarded origin replaces the Host and scheme in the steps above, allowedHosts is checked against the forwarded host, and a missing or malformed forwarded header is refused with a FORWARDED_* reason.

      The Host header (or, over HTTP/2, the request URI's authority) is the handshake's own host under either CsrfBoundary.OriginSource. X-Forwarded-* and Forwarded are never read unless CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedForwarding(ForwardedSource) is set, which only checkHandshake(String, HandshakeHosts, Map) supports. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, the scheme is right only if the container's own forwarded-header support rewrites the request URI it hands the WebSocket layer; where it does not, a wss page's handshake is refused rather than admitted on a guess.

      Parameters:
      scheme - The scheme of the handshake's request URI. Can be null, which is refused.
      hosts - Every Host value of the handshake. Must not be null.
      origins - Every Origin value of the handshake. Must not be null.
      fetchSites - Every Sec-Fetch-Site value of the handshake. Must not be null.
      Returns:
      BoundaryResult.ALLOWED, or the first rejection. A rejection message never echoes a value the handshake presented.

    • checkHandshake

      public BoundaryResult checkHandshake(String scheme, HandshakeHosts hosts, List<String> origins, List<String> fetchSites)
      Applies this boundary to a WebSocket handshake whose Host values may have been synthesised.

      As checkHandshake(String, List, List, List), except that hosts may carry the value built from the request URI's authority when a handshake over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) has no Host header. The synthesised value is judged exactly as a real one would be.

      Parameters:
      scheme - The scheme of the handshake's request URI. Can be null, which is refused.
      hosts - The handshake's Host values. Must not be null.
      origins - Every Origin value of the handshake. Must not be null.
      fetchSites - Every Sec-Fetch-Site value of the handshake. Must not be null.
      Returns:
      BoundaryResult.ALLOWED, or the first rejection. A rejection message never echoes a value the handshake presented.

    • checkHandshake

      public BoundaryResult checkHandshake(String scheme, HandshakeHosts hosts, Map<String,List<String>> headers)
      Applies this boundary to a WebSocket handshake, reading every header it needs from the handshake's header map.

      As checkHandshake(String, HandshakeHosts, List, List), with Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site taken from headers (every value, across all spellings of the name). This is the form to use when CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedForwarding(ForwardedSource) is set, because only it can see the forwarded headers; the other forms always refuse such a handshake with FORWARDED_HOST_MISSING. A forwarded header the map holds under more than one spelling is refused, because the order of its values across spellings is unknowable.

      Parameters:
      scheme - The scheme of the handshake's request URI. Can be null, which is refused.
      hosts - The handshake's Host values. Must not be null.
      headers - The handshake's headers. Can be null, which is empty.
      Returns:
      BoundaryResult.ALLOWED, or the first rejection. A rejection message never echoes a value the handshake presented.

    • checkHandshake

      public BoundaryResult checkHandshake(String scheme, HandshakeHosts hosts, Map<String,List<String>> headers, InetAddress peer)
      Applies this boundary to a WebSocket handshake whose peer address the container reported.

      As checkHandshake(String, HandshakeHosts, Map), plus the peer allow-list of CsrfBoundary.Builder.trustedProxies(String...): when it is set, the forwarded headers are believed only from a peer on it. The Jakarta WebSocket API has no peer address; a container that supplies none (Tomcat) passes null, which is never on the list. A null peer is not looked at when the list is not set.

      Parameters:
      scheme - The scheme of the handshake's request URI. Can be null, which is refused.
      hosts - The handshake's Host values. Must not be null.
      headers - The handshake's headers. Can be null, which is empty.
      peer - The address of the TCP peer, or null when the container did not report it.
      Returns:
      BoundaryResult.ALLOWED, or the first rejection. A rejection message never echoes a value the handshake presented.
